opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the gap is real but smaller than a lot of people in the U.S. assumed it would be, and it depends heavily on what you're measuring.

If you look at the absolute frontier, the very best closed models from the top American labs, they still tend to be ahead on the hardest things: long-horizon agentic tasks, complex coding across big codebases, and the general robustness you only notice after using a model every day. My rough sense is that the best Chinese models trail the best U.S. models by somewhere in the range of several months, maybe up to a year depending on the capability. That's not a huge amount of time in this field.

Where it gets more interesting is open-weight models. For a while now, the strongest open models in the world have often come out of Chinese labs, whether that's DeepSeek, Qwen from Alibaba, Kimi from Moonshot, or others. If you're a researcher or a startup that wants to download weights, fine-tune them, and run them yourself, the Chinese ecosystem has been extremely competitive and sometimes clearly ahead. That's something I care a lot about, because open models are what most of the research community actually builds on.

Benchmarks also make the gap look smaller than it is in practice. Many evaluations are saturated or can be targeted, so two models that look close on a leaderboard can feel quite different in real use. On the other side, the Chinese labs have been remarkably efficient. Working under export controls with less compute, they've produced real innovations in training efficiency, mixture-of-experts architectures, and reinforcement learning recipes that the whole field has learned from.

So my summary: the U.S. still leads at the very top, mostly because of compute and some product and post-training polish, but the lead is measured in months, not years. And in open models, the U.S. has real catching up to do. That's why I've argued we need stronger American open model efforts, because ceding that layer of the ecosystem has long-term consequences for research, for adoption, and for whose standards everyone builds on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training efficiency, architectures, and reinforcement learning, but does not say that a new modeling paradigm can produce unusually steep gains.

r002.rationale: It estimates the U.S. lead in months, but does not connect shorter Chinese release delays to a narrower gap for users.

r003.rationale: It compares frontier and open-weight models, but does not define the practically relevant gap as the difference between models people can access.

r004.rationale: It says U.S. models lead on complex coding and everyday robustness, and that benchmarks make the gap look smaller than it feels in practice.

r005.rationale: It does not cite the absence of an open-weight model with behavior comparable to Claude Code or Codex; it instead says Chinese open models are highly competitive.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say the gap is real but it's narrower than most people assume, and it depends a lot on which dimension you're measuring.

On raw frontier capability, the top closed U.S. models are still ahead. If you're talking about the very best reasoning performance, the hardest agentic coding tasks, long-horizon work, the labs with the most compute and the longest training runs still have an edge. My rough sense is that's somewhere in the range of six to twelve months, and honestly it fluctuates. There are moments where a Chinese release lands and the gap looks like three months, and then a new U.S. model comes out and it looks wider again.

But the more interesting story to me is open weights, because that's where Chinese labs have essentially taken the lead. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, the Zhipu models, MiniMax. If you're a developer or a researcher who wants a model you can actually download and run and fine-tune, the best options right now are overwhelmingly Chinese. Meta pulled back, and U.S. open efforts like ours at Ai2 are much smaller in scale. So on the open side, the "gap" is actually inverted.

The other thing I'd emphasize is efficiency. The Chinese labs have been operating under compute constraints because of export controls, and the response has been a lot of genuinely good engineering. Mixture-of-experts architectures, cheaper training recipes, aggressive inference optimization. The DeepSeek V3 and R1 moment was the clearest example, where they showed you could get near-frontier results at a fraction of the reported cost. That pressure has made them very good at squeezing performance out of less.

Where I think the U.S. labs still have a structural advantage is in the things that are hard to copy: the scale of compute, the amount of expensive post-training and RL work, and the product feedback loops from hundreds of millions of users. Those compound. It's much easier to distill or reproduce a capability once someone has shown it's possible than to be the first one to find it.

So if I had to summarize it: at the absolute frontier, the U.S. is ahead but not comfortably. In open models, China is ahead. And the thing that would actually change the picture isn't a single benchmark, it's whether the compute constraints bite harder over time or whether the Chinese labs keep engineering their way around them.

r004.rationale: It says U.S. labs have an edge on difficult agentic coding tasks, but does not suggest that their practical knowledge-work advantage may exceed what popular benchmarks show.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate benchmark performance from the experience of actually using the models. There isn’t one clean gap you can measure in months. A model can be very competitive on coding or math and still feel less reliable when you give it an ambiguous task or ask it to work through a long sequence of steps.

My broad assessment is that the leading U.S. labs have an edge at the frontier, but Chinese labs are strong competitors, particularly in models with openly available weights. And the gap varies by capability—it’s not simply that every American model is ahead of every Chinese model.

The other distinction is between catching up to a demonstrated capability and establishing the next frontier. Once someone shows that a technique works, other teams have a much clearer target. Sustaining leadership means repeatedly finding the next improvement. So I’d look at capability, cost, reliability, and how quickly each team improves, rather than reduce the comparison to a single leaderboard.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate a few things. There’s the gap between the best models, the gap between openly available models, and the gap in products people actually use. Those can look quite different.

If you’re comparing the very best models, I’d be cautious about saying China is some fixed number of months behind. A model can look extremely competitive on a benchmark and still have weaknesses in reliability, tool use, or handling a long, messy task. And the leading American labs don’t all have the same strengths either.

For open models, the competition is much closer. Chinese labs are serious competitors, and releasing strong models openly lets developers everywhere build on their work. That matters beyond any individual benchmark score.

So I’d describe it as a moving, uneven gap rather than a single ranking. The question is: which capability, at what cost, and with what level of reliability? That tells you much more than asking who’s ahead overall.
